one_liner: Pure-Go epoll/kqueue multi-reactor TCP/UDP framework; 1.4-1.95x Go net's packet rate on streaming 1KB echo.
what_it_does: gnet is a TCP/UDP/Unix-socket server (and client) framework for Go that replaces net's goroutine-per-connection model with a fixed set of event loops. You implement an EventHandler (OnBoot, OnOpen, OnTraffic, OnClose, OnTick; embed BuiltinEventEngine for no-op defaults) and start it with gnet.Run(handler, "tcp://:9000", opts...). Inside OnTraffic you read with Next/Peek/Discard and reply with Write; from other goroutines only AsyncWrite/AsyncWritev, Wake and Close are safe. It is not a drop-in for net: there is no net.Listener or blocking Read, SetDeadline returns ErrUnsupportedOp, and application protocols (HTTP, TLS, framing) are yours to write.
how_it_is_fast: Multi-reactor design: N event-loop goroutines (one per CPU with WithMulticore, optionally pinned with WithLockOSThread) each own an epoll/kqueue fd and call epoll_wait/read/write directly via golang.org/x/sys/unix, bypassing the Go runtime netpoller and per-connection goroutines; with SO_REUSEPORT each loop gets its own listener, otherwise a main reactor accepts and load-balances (round-robin, least-connections, source-addr hash). Each loop reads into one shared buffer and passes OnTraffic a slice of it, so only unconsumed bytes are copied into a per-connection elastic ring buffer, and Write goes straight to the socket, spilling to an outbound buffer only on EAGAIN. After events the loop re-polls with a 0 ms timeout plus runtime.Gosched before blocking, and the poll_opt build tag (used in the benchmark) stores the connection's attachment pointer in epoll_event.data to skip the fd-to-conn map lookup.
when_to_use: Go services holding thousands to 10k+ long-lived TCP connections with small messages (game servers, push/IM gateways, custom RPC or Redis-protocol servers) where per-connection goroutines and scheduler overhead dominate.
You own the wire protocol and are willing to write framing/codec code on top of Next/Peek/Discard.
Linux production using epoll (optionally built with -tags=poll_opt,gc_opt), or macOS kqueue.
Throughput per core matters more than tail latency, and handlers are short and non-blocking (blocking work goes to pkg/pool/goroutine, replies via AsyncWrite).
UDP servers that want SO_REUSEPORT fan-out across several event loops.
when_not_to_use: You need TLS, HTTP, WebSocket or gRPC out of the box: none is built in (TLS and io_uring are unchecked roadmap items), and the README says gnet's TechEmpower HTTP code is benchmark-only and not production-ready.
Existing net.Conn code or libraries (crypto/tls, net/http, bufio-based parsers) that you do not want to rewrite into callbacks; deadlines are unsupported.

Latency-sensitive request/response at moderate connection counts: the benchmark repo's own Fortio ping-pong run (1000 conns, 1KB) gives gnet only 1.15x Go net's QPS with a worse p99 (15.8 ms vs 10.2 ms).
Proxies or gateways relaying large streams to slow clients: there is no read backpressure, so outbound buffers grow until OOM (issue #722, closed as not planned).
Windows production: the README says the Windows build is for development and testing only.

integration.dependencies: panjf2000/ants/v2 (goroutine pool), valyala/bytebufferpool, go.uber.org/zap, gopkg.in/natefinch/lumberjack.v2, golang.org/x/sys, golang.org/x/sync
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll; syscall defs for amd64, 386, arm, arm64, ppc64/ppc64le, riscv64, s390x, mips) and macOS (kqueue) tested in CI; FreeBSD/NetBSD/OpenBSD/DragonFly only cross-compiled in CI; Windows for dev/test only
integration.thread_safety: Each connection belongs to one event-loop goroutine. Reader methods, Write/Writev/Flush, Context/SetContext and LocalAddr/RemoteAddr are not concurrency-safe and must be called inside EventHandler callbacks; AsyncWrite/AsyncWritev, Wake, Close/CloseWithCallback, Socket setters and SafeContext/SetSafeContext (v2.10.0+) are safe from any goroutine.

gotchas: Slices returned by Next/Peek point into the event loop's shared read buffer; copy them before passing to another goroutine or using them after Discard.
Calling Write or Context from your own goroutine produces 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write' crashes (issues #741, #720, #632, #577); use AsyncWrite or SafeContext instead.
Anything that blocks in OnTraffic, OnOpen or an AsyncCallback (which runs on the loop) stalls every connection on that event loop.

Do not touch a Conn after OnClose: before a fix, fd reuse could send writes to a new connection (#621); open issue #765 reports Enroll blocking forever during shutdown and leaked dup'd fds on failed Enroll.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every catalogued sibling (libhv, PhotonLibOS, Seastar, monoio, uWebSockets, Asio io_uring, etc.) is C, C++ or Rust; pick gnet when the service must stay in Go and you want an epoll/kqueue reactor instead of goroutine-per-connection. If you can leave Go or want io_uring, which gnet lacks, the C/C++/Rust siblings are the comparison set.
verified_claims_summary: The Oct 2021 chart in gnet-benchmarks (gnet v1.5.3 built with -tags=poll_opt, Go 1.17.2, GOMAXPROCS=8, 8 cores of an AMD EPYC 7K62, client and server on localhost) shows tcpkali streaming 1KB echo packet-rate estimates of 1.40-1.95x Go net across 1k-10k connections; later raw logs at 1000 connections (Dec 2021, and Jan 2022 labelled gnet v2) show about 1.36-1.41x more bytes echoed. A closed-loop Fortio ping-pong run in the same repo (Feb 2022, 1000 conns, 1KB) shows only 446k vs 389k QPS (1.15x), with better median but worse p99 latency.
status_note: Actively maintained (v2.10.0 released 2026-07-03, 2 open issues/PRs) and Apache-2.0, usable as an ordinary Go module, but the published benchmarks date from 2021-2022 and have not been rerun on current gnet or Go.
